title: Cannabis Plant Anatomy: Every Part, Root to Flower
h1: The Parts of a Cannabis Plant and What Each One Does
metaDescription: A tour of cannabis plant anatomy: seed, roots, stem, nodes, fan leaves, colas and trichome-covered flowers, and how each part connects to what is in the jar.
excerpt: From seed to sticky flower: what each part of the cannabis plant does, why only unpollinated female flowers are sold, and where top buds, popcorn, trim and shake come from.
keyTakeaways: The bud in the jar is the flower of a female plant; growers remove males because pollination and seeds lower flower quality.
Stalked trichomes on female flowers make most of the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes.
Leaves carry far less cannabinoid content than flowers: about 1% to 2% versus 16% to 20% in one study.
Top buds, popcorn buds, trim and shake come from the same plant and differ by size, density and where they grew.
body:
Cannabis plant anatomy explains a lot about what you see at the counter. Roots, stems and big fan leaves keep the plant alive, but the part that ends up in the jar is the female flower, coated in tiny resin glands called trichomes. Here's a quick tour of the parts of the cannabis plant, starting with the seed and ending at the bud, and how each one shapes what you buy.

## The seed: where cannabis plant anatomy starts

A cannabis seed is botanically a tiny fruit: a hard shell wrapped around a single seed, which holds an embryo and a small store of food. Look closely and you'll see a faint seam where the shell splits. Given moisture and warmth, the seed swells, the seam opens and a root tip pushes out first. A pair of rounded seed leaves follows, and then the familiar jagged leaves.

## Cannabis roots: taproot, fibrous and adventitious

The first root becomes the taproot, which anchors the seedling and grows downward. Thinner side roots, often called fibrous roots, branch off it in every direction to take up water and nutrients. Adventitious roots grow from stem tissue rather than from the main root, which is how a cutting, or clone, roots on its own.

## Root crown, stem and nodes

The root crown is where the roots meet the main stem. The stem holds the plant upright, carrying water and nutrients up from the roots and sugars out from the leaves. Along it sit the cannabis nodes, the joints where leaves and branches attach. New branches start at nodes, and the first flowers appear there too.

## Male, female and hermaphrodite plants

Cannabis plants are usually either male or female. Males make pollen, and females make the resin-rich flowers sold in dispensaries. Commercial growers keep only female plants and remove the males, because seeds lower flower quality. Pollination has a measurable cost: in one study, fertilized flowers had substantially lower levels of nearly all cannabinoids.

Now and then, a female plant also grows pollen-producing anthers among its flowers. These hermaphrodite plants can pollinate themselves and leave seeds in the buds, so growers watch for them closely. If you grow at home in Michigan, adults 21 and older may keep up to 12 plants per residence, out of public view and behind a lock.

## Fan leaves vs. sugar leaves

Fan leaves are the big, iconic leaves with long, saw-edged leaflets. Their job is to catch light and power the plant through photosynthesis. Sugar leaves are the small leaves tucked into the buds, named for the frosty trichomes that coat them.

Leaves hold far less cannabinoid content than flowers. In a study of three cannabis varieties, leaves carried about 1% to 2% cannabinoids, compared with roughly 16% to 20% in the flowers. That's why fan leaves are usually discarded, while trimmed sugar leaves often go into extracts.

## The flower up close: colas, bracts and pistils

What is a cola? It's a dense cluster of flowers along the top of a branch, and the main cola crowns the top of the plant. Our guide to [cannabis colas](/blog/what-is-a-cannabis-cola/) goes deeper.

Each tiny flower sits inside a small, teardrop-shaped bract, often called a calyx, which wraps around the part that would become a seed. Hair-like pistils poke out of each bract to catch pollen. They start out white and turn orange or brown as the flower matures.

## Trichomes: where cannabinoids and terpenes are made

Trichomes are the tiny resin glands that give buds their frosty look. Mushroom-shaped stalked trichomes, concentrated on female flowers, make most of the plant's cannabinoids, such as THCA and CBDA, along with its terpenes. Smaller sessile trichomes sit flat against the surface of flowers and leaves. Near the end of the flowering stage, trichome heads shift from clear to cloudy to amber, one cue growers use to time the harvest. Learn more in our [trichomes guide](/blog/cannabis-trichomes-101/).

## From plant to jar: top buds, popcorn buds, trim and shake

After harvest, flowers are dried, cured and trimmed, and the plant's anatomy shows up in the grades you see on a menu:

- **Top buds** come from the colas. They're usually the largest and densest.
- **Popcorn buds** are small buds from lower branches that got less light. Many shoppers see them as a good value; see our guide to [popcorn buds](/blog/cannabis-popcorn-buds/).
- **Trim** is the sugar leaves and small bits clipped off during trimming, usually used for extracts.
- **Shake** is the loose flower that breaks off in handling, often used in pre-rolls or sold as ground flower.

Our comparison of [bud, shake and popcorn](/blog/cannabis-bud-vs-shake-vs-popcorn/) breaks down the trade-offs. When you're ready to compare, browse [your store's menu](/shop/), and our budtenders at High Society are happy to explain what's in each jar. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Which part of the cannabis plant gets you high?
faq.a: The female flower, or bud. Its stalked trichomes make THCA, which turns into THC when it's heated by smoking, vaping or baking. Leaves contain much smaller amounts, and stems, roots and seeds contain little or none. That's why dried, trimmed flower is what you'll find in the jar, while the rest of the plant is set aside.

faq.q: Why are female cannabis plants preferred?
faq.a: Because the female flowers are the harvest. Their trichomes produce most of the plant's cannabinoids and terpenes, and growers keep them unpollinated, since fertilized flowers form seeds and test substantially lower in cannabinoids. Male plants make pollen rather than resin-rich buds, so commercial growers remove them before they can pollinate the crop.

Yes, but far less than flowers. In one study of three varieties, leaves held about 1% to 2% cannabinoids, compared with roughly 16% to 20% in the flowers. Sugar leaves near the buds carry more trichomes than big fan leaves, which is why trim often goes into extracts while fan leaves are usually discarded.

faq.q: What is a cola on a cannabis plant?
faq.a: A cola is a dense cluster of buds along the top of a branch. The main cola grows at the very top of the plant, where it gets the most light, and smaller colas form on the side branches. Buds cut from colas tend to be the largest and densest, the ones menus often call top buds.

claims.claim: The bud in the jar is the female flower; commercial growers remove males because seeds lower flower quality (takeaway, body, FAQ)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7329997/ (abstract via E-utilities, PMID 32670310): "In commercial production, marijuana plants are all genetically female; male plants are destroyed as seed formation reduces flower quality"

claims.claim: Fertilized flowers had substantially lower levels of nearly all cannabinoids (body, FAQ)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8602813/ (abstract via E-utilities, PMID 34804093): "fertilization substantially decreased the concentration of nearly all phytocannabinoids"

claims.claim: A female plant sometimes grows pollen-producing anthers; these hermaphrodites can pollinate themselves and leave seeds
claims.source: PMID 32670310 abstract: "hermaphroditic inflorescences, in which pistillate flowers are accompanied by formation of anthers, leads to undesired seed formation"; progeny after "one generation of selfing"

claims.claim: Cannabis plants are usually either male or female
claims.source: PMID 32670310 abstract: "produces male and female inflorescences on different plants (dioecious)"

claims.claim: Stalked trichomes on female flowers make most of the plant's cannabinoids (THCA, CBDA) and terpenes (takeaway, body, FAQ)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8488169/ (PMID 34616415): cannabinoids "are produced by stalked glandular trichomes located on female flowers", resin "contains cannabinoids, such as tetrahydrocannabinolic acid and cannabidiolic acid"; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31469934/: stalked trichomes "correlated with high cannabinoid levels", "strongly monoterpene-dominant terpene profiles"; flower terpenoids 1.28-2.14% vs leaf 0.13-0.28% (PMID 32094454)

claims.claim: Smaller sessile trichomes sit on the surface of flowers and leaves
claims.source: PMID 31469934 abstract: stalked and sessile trichomes "only differ in size and whether they have a stalk"; "sessile trichomes on mature flowers and vegetative leaves"

claims.claim: Leaves about 1% to 2% cannabinoids vs roughly 16% to 20% in flowers, in a study of three varieties (takeaway, body, FAQ)
claims.source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7039888/ (abstract via E-utilities, PMID 32094454): inflorescence "cannabinoids (15.77-20.37%)", leaf "cannabinoids (1.10-2.10%)", "three chemovars"

claims.claim: Stems, roots and seeds contain little or no cannabinoids (FAQ)
claims.source: Jin 2020 full text (Europe PMC, PMC7039888): "Roots contained between 0.001% and 0.004% cannabinoids", "Stem barks contained between 0.005% and 0.008%"; https://www.fda.gov/news-events/public-health-focus/fda-regulation-cannabis-and-cannabis-derived-products-including-cannabidiol-cbd (WebFetch): "The seeds of the plant do not naturally contain THC or CBD"

claims.claim: THCA turns into THC when heated by smoking, vaping or baking
claims.source: general chemistry (decarboxylation); THCA as the trichome product per PMID 34616415

claims.claim: A cannabis seed is a hard shell, the seed coat, wrapped around an embryo and food store
claims.fix: the hard shell is the fruit wall: the cannabis seed is botanically a small dry fruit (achene) around a single seed. Now: "botanically a tiny fruit: a hard shell wrapped around a single seed, which holds an embryo and a small store of food"
claims.source: https://www.delta-intkey.com/famfs/www/cannab.htm (Watson and Dallwitz, Families of Flowering Plants; WebFetch): Cannabaceae fruit "achenoconum", seed "not nutlike", endosperm "scant, or moderate"

claims.claim: On germination a root tip emerges first, then rounded seed leaves, then jagged true leaves
claims.source: general botany (radicle first; cotyledons then serrated true leaves)

claims.claim: The taproot anchors the seedling; fibrous roots branch off it to take up water and nutrients
claims.fix: precision: cannabis has a taproot system whose side (lateral) roots growers call fibrous roots; now "Thinner side roots, often called fibrous roots"
claims.source: general botany (taproot system with lateral roots in dicots)

claims.claim: Adventitious roots grow from stem tissue, which is how a cutting (clone) roots
claims.source: general botany

claims.claim: The stem carries water and nutrients up from the roots and sugars out from the leaves
claims.source: general botany (xylem and phloem)

claims.claim: Nodes are where leaves and branches attach; new branches and the first flowers start there
claims.source: general botany and grower usage (pre-flowers at nodes)

claims.claim: Fan leaves catch light for photosynthesis; sugar leaves sit in the buds, coated in trichomes
claims.source: general botany and trade usage

claims.claim: Fan leaves are usually discarded while trim often goes into extracts
claims.source: trade practice; consistent with the leaf vs flower cannabinoid figures above

claims.claim: A cola is a dense cluster of buds at a branch top; the main cola at the plant top gets the most light

claims.claim: Each flower sits in a bract often called a calyx; pistils catch pollen and turn from white to orange or brown

claims.source: grower practice, stated as a cue growers use, not as a chemistry claim
